questions.stem: The oldest of the four Vedas is the:
questions.explanation: The Rigveda — ~1,500-1,200 BCE — is the oldest of the four Vedas and one of the oldest religious texts in the world. It has 10 mandalas and 1,028 hymns. Sama Veda (musical chants derived from the Rigveda), Yajur Veda (sacrificial formulae) and Atharva Veda (spells, domestic rituals) came later. Rigveda's Book 9 is dedicated to Soma.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The famous 'Gayatri Mantra' of the Rigveda is dedicated to:
questions.explanation: The Gayatri Mantra (Rigveda 3.62.10, attributed to sage Vishvamitra) is addressed to Savitr, the 'inspirer' Sun god. Indra is the Rigveda's most-mentioned deity — god of war and thunder. Agni (fire) and Varuna (cosmic order, waters) are other prominent Vedic gods. The Gayatri's metre (gayatri chhanda) has 3 lines of 8 syllables each. a form of the Sun.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The social fourfold division (varna system) was first mentioned in which hymn?
questions.explanation: The Purusha Sukta (Rigveda 10.90) — probably a late Rigvedic addition — describes the four varnas (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) as arising from the cosmic sacrifice of Purusha's mouth, arms, thighs and feet respectively. Nasadiya Sukta (10.129) is a celebrated philosophical 'creation hymn'. Ushas Sukta hymns praise the dawn goddess.

questions.stem: The Upanishads, philosophical texts usually attached to each Veda, are primarily concerned with:

options.option_text: Knowledge of the self (Atman) and the ultimate reality (Brahman)

questions.explanation: The Upanishads (c. 800-500 BCE) — the philosophical core of the later Vedic corpus, the 'end' of the Vedas ('Vedanta') — explore the identity of the individual Self (Atman) with the cosmic Absolute (Brahman). Major Upanishads include Isha, Kena, Katha, Mundaka, Chhandogya, Brihadaranyaka. The sacrificial / ritual portions are the Brahmanas; rules for conduct are in the Dharmasutras / Smritis.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The 'Sapta Sindhu' of the Rigveda — the 'land of seven rivers' — chiefly corresponds to present-day:

options.option_text: Punjab / NW India and eastern Pakistan

questions.explanation: The Rigvedic 'Sapta Sindhava' — seven rivers — are usually taken as the Indus and its main tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) plus either the Saraswati or the Kabul. This places the Rigvedic 'Aryans' chiefly in the Punjab and NW Indian region (including today's eastern Pakistan). Later Vedic peoples shifted eastwards into the Ganga-Yamuna doab.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The 'Satapatha Brahmana', a text of later Vedic ritual, is attached to the:
questions.explanation: Each Veda has its own Brahmanas (ritual commentaries). The Shatapatha Brahmana ('of a hundred paths') is attached to the White Yajur Veda (Shukla Yajur Veda). Aitareya Brahmana — Rigveda. Tandya and Jaiminiya Brahmanas — Sama Veda. Gopatha Brahmana — Atharva Veda. The Shatapatha is a major source for later Vedic social and religious life.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The tribal assembly of the Rigvedic period, which discussed matters of common concern, was called the:
questions.explanation: Rigvedic polity had two main assemblies — the Sabha (a smaller, possibly older council of senior tribesmen) and the Samiti (a larger assembly of the tribe, often involved in electing the king). They are referred to as the 'twin daughters of Prajapati' in the Atharva Veda. 'Janapada' and 'Mahajanapada' are later territorial units of the 6th century BCE. 'Gana' / 'sangha' became tribal republics in the pre-Mauryan period.
